extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of natural philosophy / early modern science (general readers and philosophers)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository chapter on the laws of fluids (hydrostatics) and basic chymical (chemical) phenomena, using simple experiments and thought-experiments to illustrate principles and to argue for design/providence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Preſſure according to the Depth
rubrics_metrics.description: The pressure in a fluid increases with depth; the pressure at equal depths in the same horizontal plane is equal ("the Law of Preſſure according to the Depth").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via thought-experiments and consequences: if fluids behaved like accumulated solids there would be only perpendicular pressure and great confusion in houses and ships. Barometer calculation and air-pump experiments are used to illustrate how interior pressures differ and why chambers, ships, and living creatures depend on this law. Examples: barometer/mercury-height arithmetic; receiver/air-pump experiments showing life cannot persist when air pressure is greatly reduced; sand-vs-liquid (sandbank) analogy showing difference between solids and fluids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air behaves as a fluid and exerts hydrostatic pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Air acts as a fluid that exerts pressure according to the depth/column above a point; this pressure has real effects on living creatures, sound transmission, combustion, and the behaviour of mercury in barometers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Barometer-based numeric illustration: comparing mercury column heights and equivalent water/air column heights to show interior chamber pressure would be vanishingly small without fluid behaviour; consequences include inability to breathe, carry sound, or sustain fire. Air-pump experiments (creature under receiver) support argument. Used to argue necessity of the hydrostatic law for habitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrostatic paradox / lateral pressure depends on depth not quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lateral pressure exerted by a fluid on a surface (e.g., a dyke) depends only on the depth (height) of the fluid, not on the total quantity, surface area, or breadth of the fluid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with the sea/sea-dyke example: a dyke loaded by an immense sea does not bear more pressure than the pressure exerted by a local column of equal depth. Consequence: without this property dykes would be impracticable and navigation/inhabitability would be impossible. Contrasted with solid-material behaviour where pressure depends on quantity and surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluids exert upward pressure (buoyancy) supporting heavier bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Fluids press upwards as well as downwards; this upward pressure can support objects heavier than the fluid in which they are immersed, causing flotation when upward pressure exceeds the object's downward pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated by the tin-tube-and-lead experiment: a thin piece of lead placed over a tube mouth and submerged to sufficient depth is supported (floats) because the water pressure beneath (due to greater column height) exceeds the lead's weight; numerical reasoning uses relative densities and depths (lead ~12× water, deeper placement yields upward force). Also used to explain why ships float and why wood/ships would sink without this upward pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy between mechanical levers and fluid powers
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an analogy between the mechanical effects of levers and the forces/exchange of pressures within fluids; novel levers (De la Hire, Varignon) show effects analogous to fluid powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned to motivate thinking of fluid pressures in terms of mechanical advantage; used as conceptual support though the author notes analogies have limits and that fluids' behaviour is not identical to solid mechanics. Encourages consulting contemporary mathematicians for further explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method: illustrate natural laws with simple demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of small, repeatable experiments (barometer readings, air-pump trials, tin-tube & lead, mixing reagents) to make evident the laws of fluids and chymical operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific experimental recipes and observations are provided: place lead over tube mouth and submerge to specified depth; observe creatures under receiver in air-pump near barometer; mix crab-eyes (alkali) with vinegar (acid) to see effervescence. These experiments serve as accessible proofs of abstract principles and to persuade non-specialist readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attraction and Repulfion (chemical/Chymical motions at a distance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain bodies, when placed at certain distances or circumstances, move toward or away from one another without visible percussion—these actions are termed attraction and repulsion and are fundamental chymical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a class of laws distinct from percussion/striking; chymists and mathematical contemplations have made these phenomena objects of study. Invites consultation of Newton and chymical authors for collections of examples and further proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acids and Alcalies react with effervescence to form new salts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing acids and alcalies (alkalis) commonly produces effervescence and the formation of new mixed salts, often accompanied by loss or change of original properties (taste, volatility, smell).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental examples: beaten crab-eyes (alkali) + vinegar (acid) effervesce; mixing spirit of sal-ammoniac with salt-of-tartar and spirit of salt (saltpetre) leads to vigorous effervescence and new substances. The new salts may have very different properties from the reactants; effervescence and change in volatility/smell are diagnostic. These operations are used to demonstrate natural laws and chemical transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement and separability among acids and alcalies (reagent hierarchy)
rubrics_metrics.description: One acid or alkali may displace another from its compound depending on relative strengths; adding a different reagent (another acid, water, or heat) can separate previously united substances and form new salts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete chain reactions are given: spirit of sea-salt on tartar effervesces to a mixed salt; adding spirit of salt-petre draws off the acid of sea-salt and unites with the alkali, producing a burning salt-petre; subsequent addition of other acids (spirit of copperas) can again separate components. Separation sometimes requires small fire, sand heating, or dilution with water. This illustrates a practical displacement hierarchy and methods for effecting separations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acids and Alcalies are widely dispersed in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Acidic and alkaline substances are abundant across animal, plant, and mineral bodies; many natural juices, soils, salts, and residues contain or yield acids or alcalies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples enumerated: in animals (milk, whey, stomach humours), in minerals (sulphur, copperas, salt-petre, alum), in plants and fruits (unripe fruits, fermented liquors), in ashes and calcinated remains (soot, burnt shells yield alkalies). Numerous medicinal springs yield sour waters; various rocks and soils effervesce with reagents. This ubiquity grounds broad applicability of chymical laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation and regularity of natural laws as argument from design
rubrics_metrics.description: The consistent operation of innumerable small particles according to precise laws that preserve order and maintain habitability is presented as evidence of a wise director (God).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical inference rather than empirical rule: the text repeatedly argues from the necessity and beneficence of hydrostatic and chymical laws (e.g., enabling houses, ships, dykes, and the seas to be managed) to conclude a providential design. The argument links experimental demonstrations with theological reflection and moral persuasion.
